    MA3700 · AIRCRAFT STRUCTURES 1

    In-Service Loads

    #Lift, Drag, and Moment Coefficients

    where T is engine thrust and P is lift generated by horizontal stabilizer

    Center of pressure cp:

    • Average location of the pressure variation
    • Location moves as angle of attack α changes

    Aerodynamic center ac:

    • Point in which aerodynamic moment remains nearly constant with α
    • Aerodynamic forces — lift and drag, are taken to act through this point

      Lift and drag forces acting on the airfoil are replaced by corresponding lift
      and drag forces acting at the aerodynamic center with a pitch moment

    #Lift Coefficient

    💡
    L=21​ρV∞​2⋅S⋅CL​

    where ρ is air density at that altitude,
    and     S is planform area of the wing

    Lift curve provides information such as:

    • Maximum CLmax​​ and its αmax​
    • Minimum CLmin​​ and its αmin​
    • Lift slope CLα​

    #Drag Coefficient

    💡
    D=21​ρV∞​2⋅S⋅CD​

    Coefficient of drag is the sum of profile drag
    (skin friction and form) and induced drag
    caused by the generation of lift.

    💡
    CD​=CD0​​+πe⋅ARCL​2​

    where CD0​​ is profile drag constant,
    and     e is span effectiveness factor

    💡
    AR=Sb2​=cb​

    where b is wing span and c is chord length

    #Pitch Moment Coefficient

    💡
    Mac​=21​ρV∞​2⋅S⋅c⋅CM​

    where c is average chord length of airfoil,
    and     CM​ is pitch moment coefficient

    #Steady Level Flight Examples

    #Example 1

    In steady level flight, thrust required is equal to drag, since net acceleration is zero. Additionally, lift generated by the wings is also equal to the weight of the aircraft.

    V=350 km/h=97.222 m/s

    L=3900(9.81)=38259 N

    Standard Sea Level

    q=21​ρV2

    q=21​(1.225)(97.222)2

    q=5789.4 N/m2

    CL​=qSL​

    CL​=5789.4(27.3)38259​

    CL​=0.24207

    CD​=CD0​​+πe⋅ARCL​2​

    CD​=0.03+π(0.9)(7.5)0.242072​

    CD​=0.032763

    CD​=qSD​

    D=5789.4(27.3)(0.032763)

    D=5178.2 N

    Altitude of 4.5km

    q=21​ρV2

    q=21​(0.77704)(97.222)2

    q=3672.3 N/m2

    CL​=qSL​

    CL​=3672.3(27.3)38259​

    CL​=0.38162

    CD​=CD0​​+πe⋅ARCL​2​

    CD​=0.03+π(0.9)(7.5)0.381622​

    CD​=0.036868

    CD​=qSD​

    D=3672.3(27.3)(0.036868)

    D=3696.2 N

    #Example 2

    V=200 mph=89.406 m/s

    m=5000 lb=2268 kg

    S=200 ft2=18.58 m2

    q=21​ρV2=21​(1.225)(89.406)2=4896 N/m2

    CL​=qSL​=4896(18.58)2268(9.81)​=0.24458

    CD​=CD0​​+πe⋅ARCL​2​

    CL​CD​​=CL​CD0​​​+πe⋅ARCL​​

    Differentiating with respect to CL​,

    dCD​dCL​​=−CL​2CD0​​​+πe⋅AR1​

    For CD​CL​​ to be maximum, equate derivative to zero.

    0=−CL​2CD0​​​+πe⋅AR1​

    CD0​​=πe⋅ARCL​2​

    Substituting CD0​​ back into drag coefficient,

    CD​=CD0​​+πe⋅ARCL​2​

    CD​=2⋅π(0.93)(8.5)0.244582​

    CD​=0.0048175

    D=qS⋅CD​

    D=4896(18.58)(0.0048175)

    D=438.24 N

    #Acceleration Induced Inertia Forces

    Maximum loading usually occurs when an aircraft undergoes accelerations. The loads
    produced while maneuvering or encountering gusts in flight are always greater than
    the loads on an aircraft in static equilibrium.

    Inertia force Fi​ is defined as,

    💡
    Fi​=−ma

    By adding an inertial force, a dynamic problem can be converted into a static problem.
    Note that the direction of the inertia force is opposite to the acceleration of the body.

    An aircraft maneuvering with:

    • Horizontal acceleration ax​
    • Vertical acceleration ay​
    • Pitch acceleration α

    To convert into a static problem:

    • Horizontal inertia force −max​
    • Vertical inertia force −may​
    • Inertia moment −Iα

    I represents the mass moment of inertia of the body.
    Note that the inertia forces and moment are acting at the CG of the body.

    The aircraft can then be assumed to be in static equilibirum:

    • ∑Fx​=0
    • ∑Fy​=0
    • ∑MCG​=0

    Internal forces are often required to calculate the stresses of structural members at those locations of interest. Other external structural forces and inertial forces are accordingly established. The member is then assumed to be in static equilibrium.

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fx​=0,

    F−ma=0

    a=9.8125000​8000​=3.1392 m/s2

    The term ma is the inertial force, which is opposite in direction to a.

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fy​=0,

    R1​+R2​−W=0

    R2​=25000−R1​     −[1]

    Taking anticlockwise as positive ∑MCG​=0,

    F(2.2)+R2​(0.8)−R1​(3.5)=0

    3.5R1​−0.8R2​=17600     −[2]

    Substituting [1] into [2],

    3.5R1​−0.8(25000−R1​)=17600

    R1​=8744.2 N

    R2​=16256 N

    #Part (ii)

    V0​=120 km/h=33.333 m/s

    Using kinematic equation v2=v0​2+2a(s−s0​),

    0=33.3332+2(3.1392)s

    s=−176.97 m

    Displacement is taken to be positive to the right and negative to the left of the aircraft’s current position. Since the aircraft is landing in a leftward direction,
    the displacement will be negative.

    #Example 2

    Since thrust is assumed to be equal to drag, there are only vertical forces present.

    L+P=4000(9.81)+190212

    P=229452−L     −[1]

    #Internal Forces Examples

    #Example 1

    #Part (i)

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fx​=0,

    ma−Tcos10°=0

    T=cos10°gW​⋅3g​=cos10°3W​

    T=cos10°3(45000)​=137083 N

    The horizontal acceleration a=3g is replaced with the inertia force ma.

    #Part (ii)

    Let N, S, and M be the axial, shear, and moment loads respectively.

    Inertia force of section A-A: m1​a=gW​⋅3g=4500(3)=13500 N

    The horizontal acceleration a=3g is replaced with the inertia force m1​a.

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fx​=0,

    m1​a+Ncos10°−Ssin10°−Tcos10°=0

    13500+Ncos10°−Ssin10°−135000=0

    S=sin10°121500−Ncos10°​     −[1]

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fy​=0,

    Nsin10°+Scos10°−4500−Tsin10°=0

    Nsin10°+Scos10°−4500−23804=0

    Nsin10°+Scos10°=28304     −[2]

    Substituting [1] into [2],

    Nsin10°+tan10°121500−Ncos10°​=28304

    N(sin10°−tan10°cos10°​)=−660757

    N=122103 N

    S=7210.6 N

    Note that there is a moment M at section A-A but we are unable to determine
    the magnitude without being given more geometrical data such as the locations
    of the aft center of gravity and     T.

    #Example 2

    #Part (i)

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fy​=0,

    2(200)−135−ma=0

    a=135/9.81265​=19.257 m/s2

    Let muc​ be the mass of the strut.

    muc​a=9.812.25​⋅19.257=4.4167 kN

    Assume N to be pointing downwards
    and M to be an anticlockwise moment.

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fy​=0,

    200−2.25−muc​a−N=0

    N=200−2.25−4.4167

    N=193.33 kN

    Taking moments about the contact point between wheel and ground ∑M=0,

    M+200(0.15)−(muc​a+2.25)(0.15)=0

    M=−29.0 kNm

    Negative sign indicates that M is clockwise.

    #Part (ii)

    Using kinematic equation v2=v0​2+2a(s−s0​),

    0=3.52+2(19.257)s

    s=−0.31807 m

    Taking upwards as positive from the strut’s current position, a negative
    value indicates movement of the strut in the downwards direction.

    #Part (iii)

    Let mw​ be the mass of the outboard wing section A-A.

    Assume S to be pointing upwards and M to be a clockwise moment.

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fy​=0,

    S−mw​a−6.6=0

    S=9.816.6​⋅19.257+6.6

    S=19.556 kN

    Taking moments about section A-A,

    −M−(mw​a+6.6)(3.05)=0

    M=−59.645 kNm

    Negative sign indicates that M is an anticlockwise moment.

    #Airworthiness and Load Factor

    Airworthiness of an aircraft is concerned with the standards of safety incorporated in all
    aspects of its construction, ranging from structural strength to provision of safeguards.

    #Load Factor during Symmetric Maneuvers

    In a steady, unaccelerated, level flight condition, the loads are in static equilibirum.

    For vertical equilibrium,

    L+P−W=0

    For horizontal equilibrium,

    T−D=0

    Taking summation of moments about the aircraft’s CG,

    La−Db−Tc−Pl+M0​=0

    La−Db−Dc−Pl+M0​=0

    whereby M0​=21​ρV2S⋅c⋅CM0​​

    #Example 1

    Note that the tail plane lift P should be pointing downwards.

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fx​=0,

    0=D−Wsinθ

    D=5000(9.81)sin15°

    D=12695 N

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fy​=0,

    0=L−P−Wcosθ

    0=L−6500−5000(9.81)cos14°

    L=54879 N

    Taking summation of moments ∑MCG​=0,

    Assume anticlockwise as the positive direction.

    0=0.4L−4.9P−M0​

    M0​=0.4(54879)−4.9(6500)

    M0​=−9898.4 Nm

    Aerodynamic moment is in the anticlockwise direction.

    #Example 2

    Note that the aerodynamic moment M0​ is in the anticlockwise direction.

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fx​=0,

    0=D−T

    T=2500 N

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fy​=0,

    0=L+P−W

    L=40000−P

    Taking summation of moments ∑MCG​=0,

    Assume anticlockwise as the positive direction.

    0=0.2L+0.1D+2.7P+M0​

    0=0.2(40000−P)+0.1(2500)+2.7P+12500

    P=−8300 N

    The tail plane lift is pointing downwards.

    L=40000−(−8300)

    L=48300 N

    #Example 3

    M0​=21​ρV2S⋅c⋅CM0​​

    =21​(1.223)(250)2(50)(2.5)(0.032)

    =152875 Nm

    Recall that a negative pitch moment coefficient is a nose down moment.
    Thus, the aerodynamic moment     M0​ is an anticlockwise moment.

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fy​=0,

    0=L+P−W

    L=145000−P

    Taking summation of moments ∑MCG​=0,

    Assume anticlockwise as the positive direction.

    0=−0.5L+8.5P+0.3T+0.4D+M0​

    0.5L=8.5P+0.7D+152875

    0.5(145000−P)=8.5P+0.7D+152875

    Iteration 1

    Assume P is extremely small compared to L.

    L≈145000 N

    CL​=21​ρV2SL​

    CL​=21​(1.223)(250)2(50)145000​

    CL​=0.075755

    CD​=0.021+0.041CL​2

    CD​=0.021+0.041(0.075755)2

    CD​=0.021235

    D=21​ρV2SCD​

    D=21​(1.223)(250)2(50)(0.021235)

    D=40579 N

    Substituting into the moments equation,

    0.5(145000−P)=8.5P+0.7(40579)+152875

    P=−12087 N

    L=157087 N

    Iteration 2

    Assume L=157087 N.

    CL​=21​(1.223)(250)2(50)157087​

    CL​=0.082204

    CD​=0.021+0.041(0.082204)2

    CD​=0.021277

    D=21​(1.223)(250)2(50)(0.021277)

    D=40659 N

    Substituting into the moments equation,

    0.5(145000−P)=8.5P+0.7(40659)+152875

    P=−12093 N

    L=157093 N

    Comparing with the results obtained in the first iteration, the results have
    almost converged. Thus, there is no need to carry out further iterations.

    #Example 4

    • ρ=0.116 kg/m3
    • W=1.6 MN
    • cˉ=22.8
    • S=280 m2 and ST​=28 m2
    • CLα​=4.5/rad and CLαT​​=2/rad
    • CM0​​=−0.01 (Nose down moment)
    • CD​=0.03+0.1CL​2

    #Part (i)

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fy​=0,

    0=L+P−W

    L=1600000−P

    Taking summation of moments ∑MCG​=0,

    Assume anticlockwise as the positive direction.

    0=7.5L+M0​−42.5P−0.75D

    0=7.5L+21​ρV2S⋅cˉ⋅CM0​​−42.5P−0.75D

    0=7.5L+21​(0.116)(610)2(280)(22.8)(0.01)−42.5P−0.75D

    0=7.5L+1377782−42.5P−0.75D

    7.5(1600000−P)=42.5P+0.75D−1377782

    Iteration 1

    Assume L≈1.6×106 N.

    CL​=21​(0.116)(610)2(280)1.6×106​=0.26477

    CD​=0.03+0.1(0.26477)2=0.03701

    D=21​(0.116)(610)2(280)(0.03701)=223651 N

    Substituting into the moments equation,

    7.5(1600000−P)=42.5P+0.75(223651)−1377782

    P=264201 N

    L=1335799 N

    Iteration 2

    Assume L=1335799 N.

    CL​=21​(0.116)(610)2(280)1335799​=0.22105

    CD​=0.03+0.1(0.22105)2=0.034886

    D=21​(0.116)(610)2(280)(0.034886)=210815 N

    Substituting into the moments equation,

    7.5(1600000−P)=42.5P+0.75(210815)−1377782

    P=264393 N

    L=1335607 N

    #Part (ii)

    Δα=Vu​=61018​=0.029508 rad

    ΔL=21​ρV2S⋅CLα​⋅Δα

    ΔL=21​(0.116)(610)2(280)(4.5)(0.029508)

    ΔL=802418 N

    ΔP=21​ρV2S⋅CLα​⋅Δα

    ΔP=21​(0.116)(610)2(28)(2)(0.029508)

    ΔP=35663 N

    nG​=1+WΔL+ΔP​

    nG​=1+1600000802418+35663​

    nG​=1.5238

    #Example 5

    M0​=21​ρV2S⋅c⋅CM0​​

    M0​=21​(1.225)(180)2(46)(3)(0.035)

    M0​=95851 N

    Aerodynamic moment is in the anticlockwise direction
    since pitch moment coefficient is negative.

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fy​=0,

    0=L+P−W

    L=88290−P

    where P≥−9000 N since only limiting factor is maximum downwards load

    Taking summation of moments ∑MCG​=0,

    0=M0​−IW​L+IT​P

    0=95981−IW​(88290−P)+(8−IW​)P

    0=95981−88290IW​+IW​P+8P−IW​P

    P=888290IW​−95981​

    Substituting into the inequality,

    888290IW​−95981​≥−9000

    IW​≥0.27162 m

    Center of gravity of the aircraft must be located such that the distance
    between the CG and the aerodynamic center ac is at least 0.27 m.

    #Load Factor during Maneuvers

    Load factor is defined as,

    💡
    n=WL​

    Using Newton’s second law,

    L−W=may​

    L−W=gW​⋅ay​

    L=W(1+gay​​)

    💡
    n=1+gay​​

    #Banking Turn

    The wings of an aircraft are banked through an angle ϕ such that the lift vector is inclined at angle ϕ to the vertical. The vertical component of lift equals the weight.

    Let r represent the radial direction.

    Fr​=L2−W2​

    Fr​=Wn2−1​

    Using Newton’s second law,

    Fr​=mar​=gW​⋅RV∞​2​

    Wn2−1​=gW​⋅RV∞​2​

    💡
    R=gn2−1​V∞​2​

    Turn rate ω=dtdθ​=RV∞​​,

    💡
    ω=V∞​gn2−1​​

    ∑Fy​=0

    Lcosϕ=W

    n=cosϕ1​

    ∑Fx​=0

    Lsinϕ=gW​⋅RV∞​2​

    n=gRsinϕV∞​2​

    💡
    tanϕ=gRV∞​2​

    For maneuvering performance of an aircraft, it is advantageous to have the smallest possible R and the largest possible ω. This is achieved through the highest n, and
    the lowest possible     V∞​.

    #Example 1

    tanϕ=9.81(1220)1682​

    ϕ=67.02°

    n=cos67.021​

    n=2.5615

    (L+P)cosϕ=W

    L+P=cosϕW​=nW

    L+P=2.5615(133500)

    L+P=341962

    L=341962−P

    Note that n=cosϕ1​.

    Taking summation of moments ∑MCG​=0,

    Assume anticlockwise as the positive direction.

    0=−0.915L+7.625P+0.45D+M0​

    0=−0.915(341962−P)+7.625P+0.45D+72228.8

    8.54P=−0.45D+240666

    Iteration 1

    Assume L≈341962 N.

    CL​=21​(1.223)(168)2(46.5)341962​=0.4261

    CD​=0.01+0.05(0.4261)2=0.019078

    D=21​(1.223)(168)2(46.5)(0.019078)=15311 N

    Substituting into the moments equation,

    8.54P=−0.45(15311)+240666

    P=27374 N

    Iteration 2

    P=27433.25 N

    L=314528.75 N

    Iteration 3

    P=27433.37 N

    L=314528.63 N

    #Example 2

    Pull-up from dive at lowest point

    A pull-up from a dive only requires the aircraft to pitch up.

    Using Newton’s second law,

    Fr​=mar​

    L−W=gW​⋅RV2​

    L=W(gRV2​+1)

    n=gRV2​+1

    RV​=Vg(n−1)​

    ωpitch​=Vg(n−1)​

    To maximize angular velocity, minimize V and maximize n=WL​.

    Thus, the maximum lift that the aircraft can generate is L=4.8W.

    Since L=21​ρV2S⋅CL​, minimum V is achieved when CL​ is maximum.

    In steady level flight where n=1,

    L=W=21​ρVS​2S⋅CLmax​​

    VS​2=ρSCLmax​​2W​

    In pull-up maneuver where n=4.8,

    L=4.8W=21​ρVmin​2S⋅CLmax​​

    Vmin​2=ρSCLmax​​9.6W​

    Taking ratio of both equations,

    (VS​Vmin​​)2=4.8

    Vmin​=142.41 m/s

    Substituting into the angular velocity equation,

    ωpitch​=142.419.81(4.8−1)​=0.26177 rad/s

    ωyaw​=0

    Steady, correctly banked turn

    To execute a banked turn, the aircraft needs to both roll and yaw.

    n=cosϕ1​

    4.8=cosϕ1​

    ϕ=77.98°

    tanϕ=gRV2​

    ωtot​=Vg⋅tanϕ​

    ωtot​=V46.055​

    Note that V=Rω.

    To maximize angular velocity, minimize V.

    From previous part, Vmin​=142.41 m/s.

    ωtot​=142.4146.055​=0.3234 rad/s

    Resolving along yaw and roll axis,

    ωyaw​=ωtot​cosϕ

    ωyaw​=0.3234cos77.98

    ωyaw​=0.06735 rad/s

    ωroll​=ωtot​sinϕ

    ωroll​=0.3234cos77.98

    ωroll​=0.31631 rad/s

    #Pull-Up Maneuver

    For a pull-up maneuver, the flight path becomes curved in the vertical plane.

    Let r represent the radial direction.

    Fr​=L−W=W(n−1)

    Using Newton’s second law,

    Fr​=mar​=gW​⋅RV∞​2​

    W(n−1)=gW​⋅RV∞​2​

    💡
    R=g(n−1)V∞​2​

    Turn rate ω=dtdθ​=RV∞​​,

    💡
    ω=V∞​g(n−1)​

    Assume the aircraft begins to pull up from a dive when it is not at its lowest point yet.

    Using Newton’s second law,

    Fr​=mar​

    L−Wcosθ=gW​RV∞​2​

    L=W(gRV∞​2​+cosθ)

    💡
    n=gRV∞​2​+cosθ

    apply an inertia load max​.

    L=35212 N

    D=21​(1.223)(60)2(14.5)(0.09375)

    #Pull-Down Maneuver

    For a pull-down maneuver, the aircraft turns downward in a circular flight path.

    Let r represent the radial direction.

    Fr​=L+W=W(n+1)

    Using Newton’s second law,

    Fr​=mar​=gW​⋅RV∞​2​

    W(n+1)=gW​⋅RV∞​2​

    💡
    R=g(n+1)V∞​2​

    Turn rate ω=dtdθ​=RV∞​​,

    💡
    ω=V∞​g(n+1)​

    #Minimum Turn Radius and Maximum Turn Rate

    When n is large, the formulas for turn radius and turn rate can be simplified to,

    💡
    R=gnV∞​2​=g(L/W)V∞​2​
    💡
    ω=V∞​gn​=V∞​g(L/W)​

    Rearranging the lift equation,

    L=21​ρ∞​V∞​2SCL​

    V∞​2=ρ∞​SCL​2L​

    Substituting the above into R and ω,

    💡
    R=ρ∞​CL​⋅g2​⋅SW​
    💡
    ω=g2(W/S)ρ∞​CL​⋅n​​

    where the ratio SW​ is wing loading

    From the above equations, R will be minimum and ω will be maximum when both CL​ and n are maximum. Also, best performance will be at sea level as ρ∞​ is maximum.

    #Load Factor Determination

    Load factors represent an overall measure of stresses an aircraft is subjected to.

    #Limit Load, Proof Load, and Ultimate Load

    Description of the various loads:

    • Limit load — maximum load expected to experience in normal operation
    • Proof load — product of limit load and proof factor (between 1.0 and 1.25)
    • Ultimate load — product of limit load and ultimate factor (typically 1.5)

    Loads that can be easily determined:

    • Maneuver loads
    • Undercarriage loads
    • Cabin pressure loads

    Loads that are dependent:

    • Gust loads
    • Buffeting
    • Induced vibrations

    Maneuver, undercarriage, and cabin pressure loads can be determined with
    simplicity. Maneuver loads are controlled by design cases, undercarriages are
    designed for given maximum descent rates, and cabin pressures are specified.

    Gust loads depend to a large extent on the atmospheric conditions encountered
    during flight. Estimates of such loads can be obtained through extrapolation of
    experimental data.

    #Uncertainties in Design and Structural Deterioration

    • Do not pose a serious problem in modern aircraft construction
    • Actual failure loads are determined through full-scale tests
    • Corrosion and wear may be largely eliminated by close inspection
      during service and the application of suitable protective treatments

    #Variation in Structural Strength

    • Variation in structural strength between two apparantly identical components
    • Employ strict controls in manufacture of materials and fabrication of structure
    • Strict limits in chemical composition and close supervision of manufacturing

    #Fatigue

    Materials fail under fluctuating loads at a much lower stress than their normal static failure stress.

    An aircraft’s structure can still fail even
    if it possesses sufficient strength to withstand the most severe expected
    gust or maneuver load.

    #Generalized V-n Diagram

    Description of flight envelope:

    • Define the boundaries of safe operating conditions in terms of n and V∞​
    • Contains the strengths and performance limits of a given aircraft
    • Boundaries represent the maximum forces/moments that can
      be tolerated by the aircraft without any structural damage

    #Interpretation of V-n Diagram

    Description of V-n diagram:

    • Curve AB represents the positive stall line given by f(nmax​, CLmax​​)
    • Curve AE represents the negative stall line given by f(nmin​, CLmin​​)
    • Horizontal line BC represents the positive limit load factor nmax​
    • Horizontal line DE represents the negative limit load factor nmin​
    • Vertical line CD represents the maximum diving speed VD​

    Limit load factors for a given aircraft are specified by airworthiness regulations. At velocities beyond VD​, dynamic pressure becomes so large that structural damage
    may occur to the aircraft.

    Flight condition from 1 → 2 → 3:

    • Aircraft flying at velocity V1​ at an angle of attack such that CL1​​<CLmax​​
    • V1​ is kept constant and angle of attack is increased till CLmax​​ is obtained
    • Lift increases to its maximum and thus n reaches nmax​ for the given V1​
    • If angle of attack increases further, the wing stalls and load factor drops
    • Point 3 is thus unobtainable in flight — located in stall region

    Note that point 2 represents the highest possible load factor nmax​ at given V1​.
    As velocity increases,     nmax​ also increases, up to a certain value defined by the
    positive limit load factor.

    Flight condition at B (maneuver point):

    • Velocity at B is called the maneuvering velocity denoted by V∗
    • CL​ and n are simultaneously at their highest possible values
    • Corresponds to smallest possible turn radius and largest possible turn rate
    • If velocity increases from V∗ to V5​, the aircraft must fly at an angle of attack
      such that CL5​​<CLmax​​ so that the positive limit load factor is not exceeded

    At flight velocities less than V∗, it is not possible to structurally damage the aircraft owing to the generation of too much lift. At velocities greater than V∗, lift can be obtained that can structurally damage the aircraft.

    Flight condition at E (maximum velocity which flaps can be deployed):

    • Velocity at E is called the design flight speed denoted by V∗∗
    • Highest speed permissible to operate flaps

    #Example

    At Sea Level

    nmax​=21​ρ∞​V2⋅W/SCLmax​​​

    nmax​=21​(1.225)V2⋅10000×9.811.6(30)​

    nmax​=0.0003V2

    nmin​=21​ρ∞​V2⋅W/SCLmin​​​

    nmin​=21​(1.225)V2⋅10000×9.81−1.2(30)​

    nmin​=−0.000225V2

    At Altitude of 10km

    nmax​=21​ρ∞​V2⋅W/SCLmax​​​

    nmax​=21​(0.4135)V2⋅10000×9.811.6(30)​

    nmax​=0.0001013V2

    nmin​=21​ρ∞​V2⋅W/SCLmin​​​

    nmin​=21​(0.4135)V2⋅10000×9.81−1.2(30)​

    nmin​=−0.00007595V2

    #Solving Problems with V-n Diagram

    Load definitions:

    • Limit load n1​ — maximum load to be expected during service life
    • Proof load 1.25n1​ — must be withstood without detrimental distortion
    • Ultimate load 1.5n1​ — plastic deformation of components occurs at this load

    All limit loads must be absorbed without adverse permanent deformation
    of aircraft components. Any deformed parts must be replaced or repaired
    before the aircraft is cleared to fly again.

    In general, the load factor is given by,

    💡
    n=WL​=21​ρ∞​V∞​2⋅W/SCL​​

    At low speeds, nmax​ and nmin​ are dependent on CLmax​​ and CLmin​​.

    The limit load factor is given by,

    💡
    n1​=2.1+2.20462W+1000024000​

    where W is in kilograms

    #Example 1

    Velocity at A

    #Example 3

    Since we are not given details about the maneuver, we assume a general load
    factor n maneuver, whereby the aircraft moves with a vertical acceleration ay​.
    Thus, we have to include an inertia force may​ such that we can consider the
    aircraft to be in static equilibrium.

    Forces in the y-direction

    For an aircraft in level flight with ay​,
    using Newton’s second law,

    Fy​=may​

    L−W=may​

    L−W=gW​⋅ay​

    ay​=g(n−1)

    In steady level flight where ∑Fy​=0,

    L=W+may​

    L=W+mg(n−1)

    L=W+W(n−1)

    L=nW

    Moments about CG

    Taking summation of forces ∑Fy​=0,

    0=L+P−nW

    L=196000n−P     −[1]

    Taking moments about the CG,

    0=P(16.7)+M0​−L(0.915)

    0=16.7P+21​ρ∞​V∞​2S⋅c⋅CM0​​−0.915L

    0=16.7P+21​(1.225)V∞​2(27.5×3.05)(3.05)(0.0638)−0.915L

    0=16.7P−0.915L+10V∞​2     −[2]

    Substituting [1] into [2],

    0=16.7P−0.915(196000n−P)+10V∞​2

    0=17.615P−179340n+10V∞​2

    P=10181.1n−0.5677V∞​2     −[3]

    Moments about section A-A

    Since moment of the aft fuselage about the CG is known, we place a cut at
    the CG. As the cut is at the CG, the forward and aft sections will have the same weight.

    Waft​=21​(nW)=2nW​

    Waft​=98000n

    Let C be the center of gravity of the aft section.

    Let b be the distance of C from the cut.

    Taking moments about section A-A,

    0=MAA​+P(16.7)−98000n(b)

    MAA​=98000nb−16.7P     −[4]

    Note that MAA​ is the moment of the aft fuselage about the CG.

    Substituting [3] into [4],

    MAA​=98000nb−16.7(10181.1n−0.5677V∞​2)

    MAA​=98000nb−170024n+9.4806V∞​2

    MAA​=n(98000b−170024)+9.4806V∞​2

    Moment of the aft fuselage is M=600000 Nm anticlockwise when n=1.
    From the V-n diagram, cruise speed when n=1 is VC​=152.5 m/s.

    600000=98000b−170024+9.4806(152.5)2

    b=5.6076 m

    The bending moment for a general load factor n is,

    MCG​=379517n+9.4806V∞​2

    Maximum bending moment

    From the bending moment equation, maximum moment is when n and V
    are largest. From the V-n diagram, this occurs at points C and D.

    At C, substituting n=3.5 and V=152.5 m/s,

    MCG​=379517(3.5)+9.4806(152.5)2

    MCG​=1.55×106 Nm

    At D, substituting n=2.5 and V=183 m/s,

    MCG​=379517(2.5)+9.4806(183)2

    MCG​=1.27×106 Nm

    #Gust V-n Diagram

    The movements of the air in turbulence are known as gusts, and these produce changes
    in wing incidence, subjecting the aircraft to sudden or gradual increases or decreases in
    lift from which normal accelerations result.

    #Sharp-Edged Gust

    Consider an aircraft flying at a speed V∞​ with wing incidence α0​ in still air.
    After entering the gust of upward velocity u, the incidence increases by an amount,

    💡
    Δα=tan−1V∞​u​=V∞​u​

    ΔL=dαdL​Δα

    ΔL=dαd​(21​ρ∞​V∞​2SCL​)V∞​u​

    ΔL=21​ρ∞​V∞​2SdαdCL​​⋅V∞​u​

    ΔL=21​ρ∞​V∞​2SCLα​⋅V∞​u​

    💡
    ΔL=21​ρ∞​V∞​SCLα​u

    where CLα​ is the lift curve slope and u is the upward velocity of the gust

    The total change in lift however, is due to both the wings and the horizontal stabilizer.

    💡
    ΔL=21​ρ∞​V∞​SW​CLαW​​u+21​ρ∞​V∞​ST​CLαT​​u

    whereby subscript W represents the wing and T represents the tailplane

    The gust load factor Δn produced by this change in lift is,

    💡
    Δn=WΔL​=21​Wρ∞​V∞​SCLα​u​

    Assuming a steady level flight with n=1, the total gust load factor is then,

    💡
    nG​=1+21​Wρ∞​V∞​SCLα​u​

    For a downgust, the gust load factor is subtracted from the normal load factor.

    #Gust Envelope

    Gust speeds ±u1​, ±u2​, and ±u3​ are high-, medium-, and low-velocity respectively. Typical values of u1​, u2​, and u3​ are 20 m/s, 15.25 m/s, and 7.5 m/s respectively.

    Construction of gust V-n diagram:

    • Plot the positive stall line OA (also called the maximum load factor curve)
    • Compute and plot the various gust load factor lines for u1​, u2​, and u3​
    • u1​ intersects OA at B′, where altitude is assumed to be less than 20000ft
    • u2​ intersects the cruising speed line at two different points
    • u3​ intersects the diving speed line at two different points
    • Connect the intersections to form the V-n diagram

    Overlay the gust V-n diagram on the flight envelope to obtain the unsafe zones
    of gust loading that fall outside of the flight envelope. Any maneuver, gust, or maneuver with gust, outside the flight envelope can cause structural damage.

    The penetration speed VP​ is the maximum speed that the aircraft is allowed to fly in the presence of a gust, whereby the gust load factor corresponds to the positive limit load factor.

    n1​=nG​

    n1​=1+21​Wρ∞​VP​SCLα​u​

    💡
    VP​=ρ∞​CLα​u2W(n1​−1)​

    #Example 1

    Lift in Steady Level Glide

    L=21​ρ∞​V∞​2SCL​

    L=21​(1.225)(250)2(50)(0.08)

    L=153125 N

    Drag in Steady Level Glilde

    CD​=0.021+0.041(0.08)2

    CD​=0.021262

    D=21​ρ∞​V∞​2SCD​

    D=21​(1.225)(250)2(50)(0.021262)

    0=153125+P−145000

    P=−8125 N (downwards)

    0=M0​+0.5D−0.5L−9P

    M0​=0.5(153125)+9(8125)−0.5(40698)

    M0​=129339 Nm

    Change in L and P due to Gust

    ΔL=21​ρ∞​V∞​SCLα​u

    ΔL=21​(1.225)(250)(50)(4.8)(−6)

    ΔL=−220500 N

    ΔP=21​ρ∞​V∞​ST​CLαT​​u

    ΔP=21​(1.225)(250)(9)(2.2)(−6)

    ΔP=−18191 N

    L=153125−220500=−67375 N

    P=−8125−18191=−26316 N

    Gust Load Factor

    nG​=1+Δn

    nG​=1+WΔLtot​​

    nG​=1+145000−220500−18191​

    nG​=−0.64614

    #Example 2

    ΔL=21​ρ∞​V∞​SCLα​u

    ΔL=21​(1.225)(120)(80)(5)(10)

    ΔL=294000 N

    ΔP=21​ρ∞​V∞​SCLαT​​u

    ΔP=21​(1.225)(120)(15)(4)(10)

    ΔP=44100 N

    Δn=WΔLtot​​

    Δn=20000(9.81)294000+44100​

    Δn=1.7232

    Upon entering the gust, the vertical forces on the aircraft are no longer in equilibrium. There is a net force ΔLtot​=ΔL+ΔP in the vertical direction which will cause the aircraft to accelerate upwards with an acceleration at its CG.

    aCGy​​=20000294000+44100​=16.905 m/s2
